Those jobs are requeued and re-executed even though their worker is still alive, producing duplicate execution and duplicate completion/failure for the same job (and potentially double resolution of the same promise). packages/analysis-client/src/index.ts.content: `stop()` kills the processes but leaves in-flight job timers armed and never rejects pending promises. Two consequences: (1) the per-job `setTimeout` callbacks still fire after stop, calling `failEntry` + `restartWithBackoff()` and resurrecting a supervisor that was explicitly stopped; (2) the `exit` handlers run asynchronously after `this.procs = []`, observe `procs.length === 0`, and also call `restartWithBackoff()`. Any later `setTimeout(() => this.start())` can then spawn workers after an explicit `stop()`. `stop()` should clear all pending job timers, reject/resolve pending entries, and set a `stopped` flag that the `exit` handler (and `start()`) honor.

Any routed frame that is neither `progress` (with `stage`) nor `complete` (with `artifactPath`) falls through to the failure branch and rejects the job. A `progress` frame lacking `stage`, a `complete` frame lacking `artifactPath`, or any other frame type addressed to a known job id (e.g. an ack/started frame) will incorrectly fail a healthy job. Explicitly ignore/handle non-terminal frame types instead of treating them as failures.

`restartWithBackoff()` is not idempotent and races with the asynchronous `exit` handlers: `stop()` clears `this.procs` synchronously, then each killed proc's `exit` handler sees `procs.length === 0` and calls `restartWithBackoff()` again, incrementing `this.restarts` and scheduling multiple stacked `start()` calls. Also `backoffMs` is only ever doubled and never reset to `restartBackoffMs[0]` after a healthy run, so backoff monotonically escalates to the max even for isolated, widely-spaced failures. Add a restart-in-progress guard and reset `backoffMs` once the worker has been healthy.

`lastHeartbeat` is never reset when workers are (re)spawned or stopped. After a restart, the stale timestamp is still compared against `Date.now()`, so `checkHeartbeat()` can immediately declare a fresh worker unhealthy (before it emits its first heartbeat) and trigger a restart loop that never stabilizes. Reset `this.lastHeartbeat` in `spawnOne()`/`start()` and in `stop()`.

Fallback lookup by `trackId` returns the first matching entry. When the same track is analyzed again while a prior job for that track is still pending, multiple entries share the same `trackId` and messages addressed by track id can be routed to the wrong job, resolving/rejecting an unrelated promise. Prefer the unique job id for routing and treat the trackId fallback as ambiguous.

In-flight detection is derived solely from `entry.timer !== undefined`, which conflates a job that has actually been dispatched with one that was requeued after a crash (timer cleared). Combined with the concurrency/`send()` bug this makes `capacity` unreliable. Consider tracking an explicit `dispatchedTo`/`inFlight` flag on `PendingEntry` rather than inferring state from the presence of a timer.

packages/govee/src/engines/native-ts.ts.content: The previous PacingStream for this device is snapshotted but never closed before it is overwritten in `this.streams`. Since PacingStream only clears its interval and writes `arm(false)` inside `close()`, the replaced stream keeps its pacing interval alive and never disarms, leaking a timer and leaving the unit armed. Anyone still holding the old stream handle will also paint concurrently with the new stream (duplicate/interleaved arm(true)+frames on the same device). Close the existing stream before replacing it.

The one-shot stream created here is never stored in `this.streams` (nor any other collection), so: (1) `close()` cannot disarm it, and the unit can be left armed after the engine closes; (2) its `setTimeout` handle is unmanaged and cannot be cancelled; (3) repeated `segment()` calls for the same device create overlapping concurrent streams that both arm and paint, producing duplicate frames; (4) it is invisible to `metrics()`. Track transient streams (e.g. a dedicated field) so `close()` can cancel/disarm them and so a new `segment()` can supersede the previous one.

The restore timer is never stored or cancelled, and `restore` is captured from `stream.currentFrame`, which is updated by `setAll` (PacingStream sets `current = latest` on every set). A second `identify()` within `identifyFlashMs` therefore captures the white flash as `restore` (`stream.currentFrame` is already white), and its own timer restores white again — leaving the device permanently stuck on white and losing the real frame. Overlapping identifies also leave multiple uncancelled timers. Capture a stable pre-flash snapshot once per flash (and cancel/store the timer).

`resolve(deviceId)` is invoked synchronously outside any try/catch. If the resolver throws (e.g. a MAC with no registered address), the exception propagates out of `sendRaw`/`sendJson` and up into `PacingStream`'s constructor/`emit` interval callback (or into `identify`), crashing the caller or the timer callback instead of surfacing as a recorded transport error. Guard the resolution/send so resolution failures are recorded in `this.errors` like socket errors.

packages/contracts/src/index.ts.content: `beatGridSchema` is non-strict while `adaptiveBeatGridSchema` is `.strict()`, yet both are alternatives of the same union field `beatGrid` in trackModelSchema. Extra/unknown properties on a grid are therefore silently accepted for one branch and rejected for the other, making the contract's strictness depend on which union arm happens to match (and, because `beatGridSchema` is first, unknown keys also survive parsing). Make strictness consistent across both branches.

`.max(0)` forces an adaptive grid to always be an empty array, which conflicts with the superRefine rule below that reports `"adaptive must carry an empty grid"` when `n > 0`. In practice a non-empty grid with `analysisCoverage === "adaptive"` is accepted by the (non-strict) `beatGridSchema` arm of the union and only later flagged by superRefine, so the meaningful diagnostic never depends on this branch; and validating `adaptiveBeatGridSchema` directly rejects non-empty grids with a generic array-length error. Align the two so the empty-grid invariant is expressed in exactly one place.

The superRefine only enforces grid emptiness vs `analysisCoverage`; it omits range/ordering invariants that malformed data can violate without any error: `startBeat <= endBeat` for sections/phrases, events falling within the grid, and consistency between `readinessLevel` and `analysisCoverage`. Invalid state transitions thus pass the contract boundary unchecked. Consider adding these cross-field checks (or a dedicated refine) here.

`catchall(z.unknown())` makes the entire cue payload unvalidated: any properties beyond the declared optionals are accepted as `unknown` and reach consumers unchecked, so native-source schema drift (renamed/renumbered cue fields) cannot be detected at the contract boundary. Enumerate the expected cue fields (or at least narrow the catchall types) so malformed rekordbox cues fail fast.

`markers` is typed as `z.array(z.unknown())`, so malformed or unexpected Serato markers pass validation and are handed to consumers with no type information. Define a concrete marker schema (mirroring `rekordboxCueSchema`) so Serato payload mismatches are caught at the contract boundary.
